title: The Locusts Have Eaten Everything
summary: Joel describes a locust plague so severe that nothing like it has been seen before: swarm after swarm has stripped the vines, fig trees, and fields, and drought and fire have followed. He calls drunkards, farmers, priests, and elders to lament, because even the grain and drink offerings at the temple have been cut off. He summons a fast and a solemn assembly and names the disaster as a sign that the Day of the LORD is near.
story: Joel's book opens not with a vision or a call narrative but with a catastrophe that everyone in Judah has lived through. The chapter asks the community to remember it, to tell it to their grandchildren, and to see in it more than bad luck. In the larger story of the Old Testament, the covenant God made with Israel at Sinai promised rain and harvest for faithfulness and warned of locusts, drought, and famine for unfaithfulness (Deuteronomy 28:38-42). Joel stands in that covenant world and reads the plague as a summons. The chapter introduces the theme that governs the whole book, the Day of the LORD, and sets up the call to return in chapter 2.
historical:
Because Joel names no king and no datable event, we cannot say which locust plague he describes (see the introduction for the debate over the book's date, which ranges from the ninth century BC to after the exile). The setting is clearly Judah, with Jerusalem's temple functioning and its priests offering the daily sacrifices. Elders, the senior heads of families who led local communities, are the first group addressed.

Locust plagues were a recurring disaster across the Near East and North Africa. Desert locusts breed in huge numbers after favorable rains, then swarm and migrate, eating nearly every green thing in their path. Ancient texts from Mesopotamia and Egypt mention them, and they continued into modern times; a severe plague struck the land of Israel in 1915, during the First World War, and observers in Jerusalem left detailed descriptions. Joel's account of stripped bark and whitened branches (verse 7) matches what such swarms do.
cultural:
Verse 4 names four kinds of locust, using four different Hebrew words (gazam, arbeh, yeleq, and chasil). Interpreters have understood them as stages in the insect's life cycle, from hopping young to winged adult; as different species; or as poetic synonyms for successive waves. What matters is the effect: whatever one swarm left, the next consumed. The crops listed (wheat and barley, the vine, the fig, olive oil, pomegranate, date palm, and a fruit tree whose identity is uncertain, translated apple) were the staples of Judah's economy and table.

The temple depended on these crops. The law required a grain offering and a drink offering of wine each morning and evening with the regular burnt offering (Exodus 29:38-41; Numbers 28:3-8). When the harvest failed, the offerings stopped, and the daily link between God and his people seemed broken. Mourning practices included wearing sackcloth (coarse cloth made from goat hair), wailing, spending the night in lament, and fasting. A solemn assembly was a sacred gathering in which all work stopped and the whole community came before God. The image of the young woman mourning "the husband of her youth" (verse 8) pictures a betrothed or newly married bride whose husband has died, among the most bitter griefs the culture knew.
literary: The chapter is a call to communal lament built from a series of summonses: hear (verse 2), wake up (verse 5), wail (verse 8), be dismayed (verse 11), put on sackcloth (verse 13), consecrate a fast (verse 14). Each group addressed has lost something specific: drunkards their wine, farmers their harvest, priests their offerings. The locusts are described as an invading nation with lion's teeth (verse 6), anticipating the army of chapter 2. At verse 15 the lament turns into warning, and verses 19 and 20 become the prophet's own prayer, joined even by wild animals that pant for God. Verse 15 contains a Hebrew wordplay: destruction (shod) comes from the Almighty (Shaddai).

outline.t: A disaster to tell the generations
Drunkards, the land, farmers, and orchards in mourning
Priests, lament and call a fast
The Day of the LORD is near
The prophet's cry and the panting animals

doctrines.note: Joel reads a natural disaster within the covenant, as a warning that points toward the Day of the LORD. The chapter does not claim that every calamity is a direct punishment for particular sins, but it insists that disasters can call a people to examine themselves before God.

The chapter models lament as a faithful response to disaster. Grief is voiced openly, the whole community is summoned, and the prophet ends by crying out to the LORD himself (verse 19), bringing the pain to God rather than away from him.

The locusts are called "a nation" that has invaded God's land, and the Day comes "from the Almighty". Joel sees God's hand at work even in insects and weather, which means that nothing in creation lies outside his rule.

words.note: Gazam, one of the four locust words in verse 4, translated "devouring locust". The word appears to come from a root meaning to cut off, fitting insects that shear vegetation. It reappears in 2:25 when God promises to repay the years the locusts have eaten, and Amos 4:9 uses it for a locust judgment in Israel.

Shaddai, the Almighty, an ancient name for God used by the patriarchs (Genesis 17:1). Its original meaning is debated; it has been linked to mountains or to might. In verse 15 Joel pairs it with shod, destruction, in a sound play that makes the point: the devastation comes from the all-powerful God.

Atsarah, a solemn or sacred assembly. The word names a gathering set apart from ordinary work, often at the close of a festival (Leviticus 23:36). Joel calls one in a time of crisis so that the whole community, not only the priests, might stand before God and cry out.

Yalal, to wail or howl. It is the loud, public lament of mourning, and Joel uses it for drunkards, farmers, and priests alike. The repetition turns the chapter into a chorus of grief sung by every part of society.

christ: Joel 1 introduces the Day of the LORD, a theme the New Testament applies to Jesus: the day of the Lord becomes the day of his return in judgment and salvation (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10). The chapter's call to lament also has a place in Christian faith. Jesus himself wept over Jerusalem as he foresaw its destruction (Luke 19:41-44), and his teaching that famines and disasters are the beginning of birth pains (Mark 13:8) stands in the same prophetic tradition of reading calamity as a summons to watchfulness. These are thematic connections rather than predictions in Joel 1. The chapter's deepest link to Christ comes through what follows: the lament of chapter 1 leads to the call to return and the promise of the Spirit in chapter 2, which Peter proclaimed as fulfilled at Pentecost.

hard.q: Does Joel mean that natural disasters are always God's punishment?
hard.a: Joel clearly interprets this locust plague as coming from God and as a warning connected to the Day of the LORD. He stands in the covenant framework of Deuteronomy, where crop failure was one of the promised consequences of unfaithfulness. But Joel never lists specific sins that caused the plague, and his emphasis falls on the response it should provoke: lament, fasting, and turning to God. Elsewhere Scripture resists any simple formula that ties every suffering to a particular sin, as in the book of Job and in Jesus's words about the tower of Siloam and the man born blind (Luke 13:1-5; John 9:1-3). Many interpreters therefore read Joel as teaching that disasters can serve as God's summons to a whole community without claiming the right to announce, case by case, why a given disaster happened. Others emphasize that Joel's covenant setting was unique to Israel. Either way, the chapter's lasting lesson is about the response, not the calculation.

questions: Joel tells the people to pass the story of this disaster to their children and grandchildren. What hard seasons in your life or community deserve to be remembered, and what should be learned from them?
Each group in the chapter mourns what it has lost. What losses do you find hardest to bring to God in honest lament?
How can a community respond to a disaster in a way that turns people toward God rather than toward blame or despair?
